meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee'?
meta.ogDescription: Ali's signature taunt — but he didn't write it. His cornerman Drew 'Bundini' Brown coined the couplet. The verified provenance.

answer.label: Ali’s line — written by Drew ‘Bundini’ Brown
answer.sourceLine: Muhammad Ali (then Cassius Clay) chanted the couplet during the build-up to his first title fight with Sonny Liston in February 1964, and it became his lifelong signature taunt. But he didn’t write it: the words were coined by his cornerman and unofficial “speech writer” Drew “Bundini” Brown, per Brown’s biography. Ali was the performer; Bundini was the author.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Build-up to the first Sonny Liston title fight, Miami Beach, 25 February 1964
“Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee — rumble, young man, rumble!”

source.excerpt: Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee — rumble, young man, rumble!
trail: Ali chanted it during the build-up to his first Sonny Liston title fight (25 February 1964) and it became his signature taunt, per Brown’s Wikipedia biography.
The words were written by Drew “Bundini” Brown, Ali’s cornerman and one of his “speech writers” — not by Ali himself, the same source states.
The Irish Times calls Brown “the man who invented” the couplet.
source.excerptNote: The couplet is often extended as “… the hands can’t hit what the eyes can’t see,” a line also linked to Brown. Period accounts pair the core couplet with “rumble, young man, rumble.”
source.rightsNote: This is a six-word spoken slogan first heard around 1963–64. Under U.S. law individual short phrases generally aren’t protected by copyright, so no clean copyright claim attaches to the words themselves — yet as a 1964 line it equally cannot be called a pre-1931 public-domain work. Authorship of the wording belongs to Drew “Bundini” Brown.

author.name: Drew “Bundini” Brown
author.heading: About the man who wrote it
author.bio: Drew “Bundini” Brown (1928–1987) was Muhammad Ali’s cornerman and assistant trainer from 1963 through the end of his career, and one of his unofficial “speech writers.” A Florida-born showman who had earlier worked Sugar Ray Robinson’s corner, Brown supplied much of the rhyming theatre of the Ali era — most famously the couplet “Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee.”

cite.sourceCitation: Attributed to Drew “Bundini” Brown, coined c. 1963–64 and popularised by Muhammad Ali (then Cassius Clay) during the build-up to the first Sonny Liston title fight, Miami Beach, 25 February 1964. Earliest widely documented in period press coverage; authorship recorded in Brown’s biographical record.

misattribution.heading: The authorship mix-up
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the most famous things Muhammad Ali ever said — and he genuinely said it — but he is almost universally credited as its author, which is not right.

items.scope: As the author of the words
items.why: Ali chanted the couplet and made it globally famous, so it is nearly always printed as his own coinage. In fact his cornerman Drew “Bundini” Brown wrote it — Ali was the performer, not the author, per Brown’s biography.

misattribution.truthLine: Ali spoke it and immortalised it; Drew “Bundini” Brown coined it — The Irish Times calls him “the man who invented” the couplet.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In February 1964 a 22-year-old Cassius Clay was a heavy underdog against champion Sonny Liston. The taunting butterfly-and-bee chant, delivered through the weigh-in and press build-up, was part of the psychological theatre around the bout — which Clay won to take the heavyweight title before announcing his conversion and name change to Muhammad Ali.
Brown, who had worked Sugar Ray Robinson’s corner before Ali’s, supplied the rhymes; Ali supplied the delivery. Their partnership produced the defining catchphrase of 20th-century boxing.
detailsBody: The best-known short form is simply “Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee.” Contemporary accounts attach “rumble, young man, rumble!”, and a longer boast — “the hands can’t hit what the eyes can’t see” — is also associated with Brown and Ali’s corner routines.
context.pull: Ali performed it. Bundini wrote it.
